spoken: On the 22nd of October, 1956, students at a Budapest university drew up sixteen demands.
They wanted Soviet troops out, the work norms revised, the farm deliveries changed and the old coat of arms back.
Behind every point lay something that millions of Hungarians knew from their own lives.
The next day, their march became a revolution. To see why, we go back seven years.
By 1949, Hungary was a one-party state, run by Mah-chahsh Rah-koshee and his Hungarian Workers' Party.
Its fist was the State Protection Authority, the AVH, the political police.
It worked from 60 Ahn-drah-shee oot in Budapest, a building the fascist Arrow Cross party had used before it.
From 1950 it answered to the government on paper, but in practice to Rah-koshee alone, with Soviet advisers at its side.
Between 1950 and 1953, by the 1956 Institute's count, it took proceedings against some 650,000 people.
That was in a country of about 9.2 million. Its informers sat in offices, factories, schools and blocks of flats.
No one knew, witnesses later told the United Nations, where their words would be repeated half an hour later.
A law of 1952 even punished anyone who shunned an informer, with up to six months in prison.
In its cells, prisoners were beaten, starved and threatened until they signed confessions.
Not even Communists were safe. In 1949 Lah-slaw Royk, a former interior minister, was executed on invented charges.
The AVH did not even need a court. It could simply intern people, holding them without any trial.
Peasants branded kulaks, Social Democrats, churchmen and so-called class aliens were held in camps.
There were camps at Kish-tar-cha, Tissa-lurk and Kah-zints-bar-tsee-kah, and the most feared of all, Rechk, in the Maht-ra hills.
At this secret camp, opened in 1950, some 1,200 to 1,300 men at a time broke stone in a quarry, by former prisoners' counts.
Whole families were taken too. Before dawn on the 23rd of June, 1950, AVH men and police woke families near the southern and western borders.
That night 2,446 people were taken to closed labour camps on the Hor-toh-bahj plain. By 1953 there were twelve.
When the camps closed in 1953, official records counted 7,281 people released, and more had been taken.
In 1951 the regime turned on Budapest itself, expelling 12,704 people, former nobles, officers and officials with their families.
They were sent to 138 villages in the east and lodged in strangers' houses, often a kulak family's.
And children labelled class aliens could be barred from further study.
Meanwhile the regime set out to turn a farming country into a land of iron and steel.
The first five-year plan began in 1950. After war broke out in Korea, Stalin demanded more arms, and the targets soared.
Planned investment rose from 27.6 to 85 billion forints, and about nine-tenths of industry's share went to heavy industry.
In the factories, pay depended on the norm, the output that counted as a day's work.
The norms kept rising. At the Eekaroosh bus works, the new norms of 1950 cut average pay by 35.5 percent.
Workers were also pressed to lend the state at least a month's pay every year, in so-called Peace Loans.
From January 1951, six years after the war, food was rationed again.
By 1952, real wages had fallen to about two-thirds of their pre-war level, by the historian Ignahts Rom-shich's figures.
In 1954 the trade unions' own survey found a third of wage earners below the subsistence minimum.
In the villages, peasants owed the state compulsory deliveries of grain, meat and other produce, at low fixed prices.
The quota was set by the land, not by the harvest, so a bad year did not lower it.
Anyone farming more than 25 holds, about 14 hectares, was branded a kulak, a rich peasant. In 1949 there were 61,922 of them.
Kulak families got the heaviest quotas. In 1951 they had to deliver goods worth 700 to 1,100 kilograms of wheat a hold.
That year, the best of the period, the average wheat harvest was 970 kilograms a hold.
Brigades searched cellars and lofts for hidden grain. People called it attic sweeping.
From 1948 to 1955, almost 200,000 people were convicted of crimes against public supply, by official statistics.
Even Ishtvahn Dobee, the regime's own head of state, later said the villages had had many times more reason to complain than the towns.
Behind the regime stood the Soviet Union. Its army had entered Hungary fighting Germany in 1944 and 1945, and stayed.
The 1947 peace treaty let Soviet troops remain, to guard their army's lines to its zone in Austria.
In May 1955 a treaty ended Austria's occupation. The day before, the new Warsaw Pact had given the troops a fresh reason to stay.
Before October 1956, the UN committee was told, about 20,000 Soviet soldiers and 600 tanks were in Hungary.
Hungary paid, too. The 1945 armistice made it deliver goods worth 200 million dollars to the Soviet Union.
Trade deals with Moscow were kept secret. Uranium was mined near Paych, and people believed it went to the Soviet Union.
Soviet power showed in everyday symbols. In 1949 a Soviet-style emblem with a red star replaced the Koshoot coat of arms.
Soldiers wore uniforms modelled on the Soviet ones, and Russian was a compulsory subject at school.
The 15th of March, the anniversary of the revolution of 1848, was no longer a holiday, just an ordinary working day.
The UN committee found the Soviet soldiers themselves not personally unpopular. People resented the power that kept the regime in place.
Stalin died in March 1953. Under a new prime minister, Im-reh Nodge, the internment camps were closed and many prisoners came home.
But the AVH remained, Rah-koshee still led the party, and the fear stayed.
By 1956, workers, peasants, students and writers all had grievances, and the students' sixteen points took them up almost one by one.
Point one asked for all Soviet troops to leave, and point eight for the truth about reparations and uranium.
Points nine and ten asked for the norms to be revised, a minimum wage, and the deliveries put on a new basis.
Points eleven and twelve asked for the political trials to be re-examined, for free speech, and for the personnel files to be destroyed.
Points thirteen and fourteen asked for Stalin's statue to go, the Koshoot arms to return, and the 15th of March to be a holiday again.
And everywhere, people demanded one thing more, that the AVH be disbanded.
An eighteen-year-old student later put it simply to the United Nations. We wanted freedom, and not a good comfortable life.
Between Stalin's death and October 1956 lay three years of hope and disappointment. That is the road to the 23rd of October.
